families.s: HSE integrated health and safety management for food and drink manufacture
families.t: sector management, leadership, hazards, occupational health, workers, supervisors, practical controls, review
f: HSG252 is HSE's one-stop reference for health and safety in food and drink manufacture.
The guidance is intended for workers, supervisors, managers, directors and health and safety representatives.
It covers the main safety and occupational-health hazards in the sector.
It gives practical advice on managing the associated risks.
Food and drink manufacture includes around 30 distinct sectors.
Examples include bakeries, meat and poultry processing, drinks, dairy, fish, chilled foods, vegetables and milling.
The guidance was revised with the Food and Drink Manufacture Health and Safety Forum.
The revised guidance places increased emphasis on occupational health.

families.s: HSE safeguarding and safe cleaning of food-process conveyors
families.t: flat-belt conveyors, in-running nips, trapping points, guards, interlocks, cleaning, blockages, training
f: Conveyors account for more food and drink machinery accidents than any other machine class.
Most conveyor injuries identified by HSE involved flat-belt conveyors.
Common hazards include in-running transmission parts and traps between moving and fixed parts.
Many accidents occur during foreseeable production, cleaning and blockage-clearing tasks.
Hazards can be controlled by design, fixed guards or interlocked removable guards.
Interlocked guards can support frequent hygienic cleaning while preventing operation with guards removed.
Daily and routine cleaning should follow a formal safe system of work.
Workers should be trained for production, cleaning, isolation and blockage-clearance tasks.

families.s: HSE safe design and intervention controls for packaging and palletising machinery
families.t: packaging machines, palletisers, depalletisers, wrapping, stored energy, unexpected movement, access, isolation
f: Packaging machinery is widely used in food and drink manufacturing.
Severe or fatal injuries can occur during use, maintenance or blockage clearance.
Palletiser injuries often occur when people enter the machine and become trapped by moving parts.
Unexpected movement of transfer heads, sweepers or pushers increases the risk.
Falling loads and sudden release of jammed products or pallets are foreseeable hazards.
Stored pneumatic or hydraulic energy should be released before intervention.
Access points should be guarded or interlocked against dangerous movement.
Equipment purchasing should specify health, safety, hygiene and noise requirements and verify delivery against them.

families.s: HSE workplace-transport controls in food and drink factories
families.t: fork-lift trucks, pedestrians, reversing, loading bays, tankers, tail lifts, tipping, visiting drivers
f: Workplace transport is a major cause of fatal injury in food and drink manufacture.
Workers are injured by fork-lift trucks and other vehicles in factories and yards.
Reversing is a recurring factor when pedestrians are struck.
Falls from vehicles and trapping between vehicles and fixed structures are significant hazards.
Top access to grain vehicles and tankers should be eliminated where controls can be located at ground level.
Loading-bay arrangements should prevent trailers departing while lift trucks are still entering them.
Tail-lift trapping points and roll-cage falls require design and operating controls.
Tipping vehicles need stable ground, suitable equipment and driver instruction for sticky or shifting loads.

families.s: HSE prevention of falls from height in food and drink manufacture
families.t: ladders, vehicles, machinery, platforms, stairs, roofs, sampling, cleaning, permanent access
f: Falls from height are a major cause of fatal and serious injury in food and drink manufacture.
HSE investigations identify ladders, vehicles, machinery and platforms as common fall locations.
Maintenance, cleaning, checking and sampling frequently create access-at-height tasks.
The need to work at height should be designed out where possible.
Sampling and control points can often be placed at ground level.
Regular access should use permanent stairs and platforms with edge protection.
Temporary access equipment should be selected for the task rather than using whatever is available.
Workers should never be lifted on bare fork-lift forks or improvised pallets.
